nameStory: The Arrowhead Spiketail gets its name from the distinctive arrow-shaped markings on its abdomen, which point toward its tail like fletching on an arrow. The "spiketail" part comes from the female's prominent ovipositor - a spike-like egg-laying tube that extends from her tail end like a medieval weapon.
description: The Arrowhead Spiketail is a large, impressive dragonfly with a robust body and powerful flight. These dragonflies measure about 3 to 3.5 inches long with a wingspan reaching nearly 4 inches. They have golden-brown eyes, a dark thorax (middle body section) with pale stripes, and a black abdomen decorated with distinctive yellow arrow-shaped spots. Like all spiketails, they're strong fliers that patrol territories along streams and forest edges.

idTips.label: Arrow-shaped abdominal spots
idTips.description: Look for bright yellow triangular markings along the black abdomen that clearly point toward the tail, resembling arrow fletching or chevron stripes

idTips.label: Large golden-brown eyes
idTips.description: The compound eyes are noticeably large and colored warm golden-brown to amber, meeting briefly at the top of the head

idTips.label: Dark thorax with pale stripes
idTips.description: The middle body section appears dark brown to black with two prominent yellowish stripes running down the sides

idTips.label: Patrol flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in regular patrol routes along stream corridors, hovering momentarily before darting to new perches with strong, deliberate wingbeats

idTips.label: Female's prominent ovipositor
idTips.description: Females have a distinctive spike-like egg-laying tube extending from the abdomen tip, visible even in flight

habitat: Arrowhead Spiketails prefer clean, fast-flowing rocky streams and small rivers in forested areas throughout New England's hills and mountains. They're often found where streams have gravel or cobble bottoms with good water quality, typically in elevations from sea level to about 2,000 feet. Look for them along wooded stream corridors where dappled sunlight filters through the canopy.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with peak emergence in early June. Fresh individuals have the brightest coloration and are most active during warm afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Prime time for spotting adults from June through August. Males patrol territorial beats along streams while females visit water to lay eggs in sandy stream bottoms.
seasonality.fall: Flight season typically ends by early September, though a few stragglers may persist into mid-September during warm years.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent; larvae overwinter in stream sediments for 3-5 years before emerging as adults.

funFact: Arrowhead Spiketail larvae are among the longest-lived dragonfly nymphs in New England, spending up to five years burrowed in stream sediment before emerging as adults - meaning the dragonfly you see today started life when Obama was still president!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spiketails, but the distinctive arrow-shaped yellow spots pointing toward the tail are unique among New England species. Remember: "Arrows point the way" - if the yellow markings clearly point toward the tail like arrows, it's an Arrowhead Spiketail.
compareHints: Among its spiketail relatives, the Arrowhead Spiketail is distinguished by those distinctive arrow-shaped abdominal spots - Delta-spotted Spiketails have triangular spots that don't point directionally, while Twin-spotted Spiketails have paired round spots rather than arrows. Tiger Spiketails have more complex banding patterns rather than simple directional arrows.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Delta-spotted Spiketails have more distinct, triangular yellow spots than the Twin-spotted Spiketail's paired round spots, and their spots are more numerous than the single large spots of Arrowhead Spiketails.

Twin-spotted Spiketails are distinguished from Delta-spotted Spiketails by having two round spots per segment rather than triangular markings, and from Tiger Spiketails by their smaller size and less bold yellow stripes.
